Storm reviews: the strongest lows, one at a time

← Back to the archive
ERA5 proxy, not direct observation. ERA5 is a weather model re-run over past years and blended with the observations available. Every storm here was found in ERA5 by the project’s pipeline A tracker, and every chart is drawn from ERA5 fields. 17 of the 30 are before the 2004–05 season, where no archive record exists; the other 13 are since then, and are still read here from ERA5. ERA5 smooths the very strongest winds and pressure minima, so real peaks may be stronger. These are case studies, not a trend: nothing here says whether such storms are becoming more or less common.
What this page shows

The 30 deepest lows ERA5 found, 15 in the Atlantic and 15 in the Pacific, ranked by lowest central pressure. Each has its own page that walks through how the storm developed: how fast it deepened, what the upper-level pattern looked like, where the fronts and the low-level jet were, which part of the storm had the strongest wind, and whether OPC carried it as hurricane force. Use it to compare the setup of a storm you are watching with how the strongest storms on record developed. The list is ranked by pressure, so it is not a list of the strongest winds.

Hours at HF strength is the number of 6-hourly positions with a gust index of at least 71.7 kt, times six. Peak gust index is the highest gust-index value over the storm’s life.

How the storms were chosen and drawn (method)

The storms are the ones with the lowest ERA5 central pressure in each basin among the 1979–2025 tracks of pipeline A (the project’s ERA5 storm tracker, research/era5/hf_history), taken in order of pressure from the lowest. Tropical-cyclone-flagged tracks are left out (three Pacific tracks, among them 30 Oct 1989 and 3 Oct 1981, which would otherwise rank second and third), and one Pacific storm from the 2024–25 season is left out because the weather-map fields used here end in January 2023. The rank shown is the rank among all tracks, so some numbers are missing. Ranking is by pressure alone, so the list is not a list of the strongest winds.

Central pressure, position and gust index come from the 6-hourly pipeline A fixes. The gust index is the highest ERA5 10 m gust over ocean within 800 km (about 430 nm) of the low. Each review also uses WeatherBench2 ERA5 at 1.5° for the 250 hPa jet, 300 hPa divergence, 500 hPa vorticity advection and Hart’s cyclone-phase-space structure measures (frontal against symmetric, cold core against warm core), and at 0.25° for the maps (sea-level pressure, 500 hPa height, 250 hPa wind, 850 hPa temperature, 925 hPa wind) re-centred on the storm. The gust swath and the storm-relative wind field use ERA5 hourly instantaneous gusts every 3 h over the 72 h window. The 24 h fall is the change in central pressure over the previous 24 h at each 6-hourly fix; the bomb line is 24 hPa in 24 h at 60°N, scaled for other latitudes by sin(latitude)/sin(60°). OPC warns on sustained winds; the gust index is a proxy for that, not the same thing. Where OPC’s archive has the storm, its fixes are matched by time and position (within 200 nm) and shown as agreement, not verification.

Read with care. ERA5 proxy throughout, never validated for storms before the archive begins. Before 2001 the gust index drifts upward at fixed storm depth, so gust numbers for the 1980s and 1990s storms are less reliable than their pressures. Not independently re-checked: how closely these ERA5 pressures match the observed minima of the named storms.

Seasons run 1 June to 31 May. Fields: WeatherBench2 ERA5 and ARCO-ERA5 (Google Cloud public data). Back to the archive
